newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK Oct manufacturing output at 18-month high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK Oct manufacturing output at 18-month high.

text.p: British manufacturing output rose for the fifth month in a row in October to its highest level in 18 months, said a leading business survey published on Friday.
The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said October also saw the first significant increase in manufacturing employment since March 1995.
Its purchasing managers' index (PMI) rose to a seasonally adjusted 54.5 percent in October from 53.5 percent in September.

"The latest rise in output was driven by an increase in the rate of growth of new orders. This was the fifth successive monthly improvement in order books and, as in recent months, orders for consumer goods showed the greatest increase," the CIPS said.

"However, the survey also found demand to have spread more evenly across manufacturing in October, with stronger demand for investment goods leading to the sharpest increase in output of capital goods seen since February 1995."
The survey, based on questionnaires sent to 310 industrial companies, is seen as an accurate barometer of developments in manufacturing that are usually reflected in later official statistics.
Prices fell overall in October, but the survey showed "tentative signs of a tightening of price and supply conditions."
The October survey was conducted before an unexpected 1/4-point increase in official interest rates to 6.0 percent on Wednesday to choke off future inflation as economic growth gathers steam.

Economists said the rate rise, which sent sterling soaring to a 2-1/2 year high on foreign exchange markets, would make life harder for manufacturers in the coming months and the PMI might not remain so buoyant.
"The upturn is still quite modest and the strength of the pound will be doing manufacturers no favours at all -- neither will the base rate hike," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

The Treasury's six-member panel of independent economic advisers, in their pre-budget report to Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on Friday, said inflation was likely to be at or below his 2.5-percent target at the end of 1997.
But they added "Five of us believe that strong demand growth will put upward pressure on inflation during 1998."
The advisers, known as the "wise people," gave the Clarke conflicting advice on his last pre-election budget, which will be unveiled on November 26.

Three advisers recommended a modest tightening of fiscal policy and two urged substantial cuts in government borrowing. The lone dissenter, Liverpool University's Patrick Minford, urged Clarke to slash taxes by 12 billion pounds.
All six of the economists expected economic growth to rise to more than 3.0 percent next year.

Tim Congdon, a strict monetarist, warned the governent that the financial stability it had achieved in the early and mid-1990s would be in jeopardy if it did not cut borrowing and raise interest rates further.
"The economy is once again on the threshold of a business cycle which will lead to higher inflation in the late 1990s," he wrote. "The period of stability has come to an end."
